analysis.one_liner: Creates independent ethics and investigative offices inside the Supreme Court to police justices' conduct.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the last weeks of the 118th Congress, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up two new offices inside the Supreme Court: one to give justices formal advice on ethics rules like gifts, financial disclosures, and conflicts of interest, and one with subpoena power to investigate ethics complaints against justices. It would also require yearly reports to Congress on the ethics advice given and require investigations to be shared with congressional committees. The bill was introduced in November 2024, weeks before the Congress ended, and the Judiciary Committee never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who want a Supreme Court that polices itself with real oversight rather than relying on each justice's judgment. The bill would create paid staff whose job is to advise justices on gifts, disclosures, and recusals, and a small investigative team that could subpoena records and witnesses when a complaint is filed. Congressional committee chairs would gain a steady stream of reports on the Court's ethics practices, and federal prosecutors would be alerted if an investigation turned up evidence of a crime.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public, via an accountable Supreme Court

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates an Office of Ethics Counsel inside the Supreme Court to advise justices and their spouses on financial disclosures, gifts, political activity, conflicts of interest, and recusal, and requires every justice to take biannual ethics training.

It creates an Office of Investigative Counsel with the power to issue subpoenas, backed by contempt of court, to investigate ethics complaints against justices arising from their own conduct or that of their spouses and dependents.
The ethics office must report to Congress each year on how often advice was sought, what topics came up, what remedies were recommended, and how often justices did not follow the advice.

Investigative reports must be made available to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees and other oversight committees within 10 days, and the counsel must notify the Attorney General if there are reasonable grounds to believe federal criminal law was violated.

The new counsels could not be people already employed by the Court, would serve staggered fixed terms of six years, and could be fired only for cause — terms designed to keep them independent of the justices they review.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the new offices, with the chief counsels paid at least $225,000 a year and other counsels at least $180,000. Justices and the Court itself would bear the real cost: for the first time their conduct could be formally investigated with subpoena power, and their ethics decisions would be documented in reports to Congress. The Chief Justice would also take on the administrative burden of appointing and housing the new offices.

drawbacks.text: The bill only 'authorizes' the Chief Justice to establish the offices rather than requiring it, so a reluctant Chief Justice could decline to stand them up at all.

Members of the public could not file complaints: only congressional leaders — Judiciary chairs and ranking members, the Senate party leaders, and the House Speaker and minority leader — could trigger an investigation.

The Chief Justice keeps the sole discretion to release an investigative report to the public; the offices must share reports with Congress, but nothing in the bill forces publication, and when the Chief Justice himself is the subject the report goes to another justice, not to anyone outside the Court.

The offices recommend remedies like recusal or divestment but have no power to impose them; the only teeth in the bill is contempt authority for refusing a subpoena, so a justice could ignore findings without penalty.

Because the offices sit inside the Supreme Court and answer to the Chief Justice, a good-faith critic could object that Congress structuring the Court's internal discipline raises separation-of-powers questions — the bill itself includes a severability clause anticipating a court might strike part of it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but partial: the bill builds the first formal ethics-advice and investigation machinery aimed at the nine most powerful judges in the country, at a modest taxpayer cost of a few staff salaries. But its design leaves the Chief Justice in charge of whether the offices exist, who runs them, and whether findings become public, and it gives ordinary citizens no way to file a complaint. It would have been a meaningful start with built-in limits, not a full accountability system.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate's final two weeks, referred to the Judiciary Committee, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker and five Democratic colleagues introduced the Supreme Court Ethics and Investigations Act on November 21, 2024, seven weeks before the 118th Congress expired.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary — the standard first stop for a Senate bill.

No further action ever appears in the record: the Judiciary Committee held no hearing or markup, the bill never reached the Senate floor, and when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill died.
No Republican senator sponsored or cosponsored the bill; all six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The nine Supreme Court justices are better off: the Court continues to police its own ethics under a code of conduct with no outside investigator, no subpoena power, and no required reporting to Congress. The congressional leaders who never acted also avoided a vote on an issue that pits Congress against the Court.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The justices; the Court keeps self-policing

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited five Democratic colleagues to cosponsor it in the Senate's final weeks.

for.name: 5 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senator joined before it died.

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the record shows no action after the referral.

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Offered no support; none of the 49 cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Senate Democrat — 6 of the caucus's 52 members — and no Republican signed on; there was never a vote to measure the split more precisely.

industries.note: Justices would lose their unreviewable control over ethics questions: their conduct could be investigated with subpoenas and their advice-seeking and refusals documented in annual reports to Congress. But even under the bill the offices exist only at the Chief Justice's discretion, are appointed by him, and he alone decides whether investigative findings become public — so the Court keeps the gatekeeping role the bill was meant to strip, a reminder of how incumbents shape oversight of themselves.
